a2_ward: Inside the crown gate, Kar Ashen's outer ward is not a ruin. It is inhabited: lamps lit on every corner at midday, a tally-yard working, a market open, four hundred people going about a morning under a mountain. Nobody runs. Nobody raises an alarm. Two children stop to look at the company and are called away by name.
e_a2_ward_1: The crown gate is reached, the ward is seen, and the road is taken back down inside the hour. It is a decision Thane will accept and enter in the record without comment. It is also four hundred people the company looked at and left, and nobody in the Ninth Sword ever manages to describe them to anybody.
a2_gatehouse: The gatehouse stair inside the arch is manned by two gate wardens in cloaks that fit them properly, with a signing book on a lectern. A queue of ward children waits beside them to have their lamps refilled from a common reservoir. One of the wardens holds out a pen and asks, politely, for the company's number.
a2_gatehouse_a: The book is signed and countersigned by a gate warden who reads the entry twice and checks the pack; then he writes a number in the margin against it. The number is not the number of people in the company, and when he is finished he blots it and turns the book face down.
a2_gatehouse_b: The question about who signs above them is answered without hesitation and without resentment: the yardmaster, and above him the chapel, and above the chapel the crown clerk. That clerk has held the office since this warden's grandfather was on this gate. He says it the way a man recites a chain of command he trusts.
a2_gatehouse_c: Nine ward children with nine lamps explain the refill rota with the patience of people who have never once been asked about it; two of them argue about whose turn the ninth lamp is. The eldest settles it by saying that the ninth lamp is not anybody's turn, and none of them finds that strange.
e_a2_gatehouse_1: A refusal to sign a signing book inside a working city, in front of two gate wardens and thirty witnesses who all stop what they are doing. The ward does not need violence. It has a gate, the company is inside it, and the crown clerk's household arrives at the gatehouse before anybody has reached the second street.
e_a2_gatehouse_2: The question about the number in the margin is asked, and a gate warden answers it honestly while reading his own entry upside down. It is the number the crown clerk requires against an arrival, he says, and it is always the same number, and the number is nine. Then he asks the company to wait.
a2_wheelhouse: The gate's wheelhouse holds a dwarf capstan the size of a small room, oiled this week, which closes the crown gate, and its pawl is chained back with a Warden chain, and the chain has been cut once and mended with a Guild splice. Nothing else in the room has been touched in a century.
a2_wheelhouse_a: The ratchet is jammed with the moor-iron pick and a wedge of dwarf oak, quietly, in four minutes. It is the single most useful four minutes anybody spends in the outer ward. Whatever else happens now, nobody in Kar Ashen can shut the crown gate behind the company without a mason and an afternoon.
a2_wheelhouse_b: The Warden chain is examined properly: cut once with a cold chisel and mended with a Guild splice. That dates the cutting to this spring and the mending to the same week as a Guild survey whose surveyor is on the Guild's own missing list, which is a coincidence Vurma refuses to call one.
e_a2_wheelhouse_1: The pawl is dropped on a dwarf capstan the size of a room, and the crown gate closes with a noise that the whole ward hears and the whole city below it feels. It announces, to four hundred people, that somebody has arrived who does not want that gate open. They respond to it as a municipal matter.
a2_foundry: The foundry under the ward wall has eleven inches of standing water on its floor and four furnaces that have been cold since the founding. There is something living in the casting pit at the far end. The ward feeds it on the ninth, from a bucket, on a rota, and the rota is chalked on the wall by the door.
a2_foundry_a: A fast crossing of a flooded moulding floor, with something coming out of the casting pit behind at a pace that suggests it has done this many times and expects to be outrun. It does not hurry. It is still coming when the company reaches the slag door, and it stops at the doorway as though the doorway were a rule.
a2_foundry_b: Round by the pattern shop, which is dry and full of nine-hundred-year-old casting patterns for key-irons in every gauge the Compact has ever used, hung in order on the wall. At the far end it opens onto the foundry chimney's base, and the chimney has iron staples in it going up into the dark.
a2_foundry_c: The ward's own offering is put down at the pit's lip, the way the lamp-children do it, and the arrangement is accepted without complaint. Eleven minutes of walking past a casting pit follow. Kettle counts the steps out of habit and stops at nine, and starts again from one, and nobody asks her to explain.
e_a2_foundry_1: The casting pit is emptied with the ward's own pumps to see what has been in there, which takes two hours of pumping and is a reasonable use of an afternoon. In the last four inches the company gets its answer. It is standing in a drained pit on a flooded floor when the answer arrives at the ninth hour.
e_a2_foundry_2: A doorway is held on a flooded moulding floor instead of running, which is the correct tactical choice against nearly everything. It is the wrong one against something that has been fed at a fixed hour for nine hundred years and has never once had to chase anything anywhere.
a2_slag: The slag heaps behind the foundry are warm, nine hundred years deep, and sorted. Founding-gauge blanks lie tipped out among the slag where the mint has been discarding rejects since before the legion, and a tally board at the yard gate records how many were tipped in each century, in nines.
a2_slag_a: Four reject blanks dug out of warm slag, each mis-struck in a different way and each still heavy and cold in the hand. Ilsabet lays them out that evening in the order of their errors and says that whoever cut them was learning, and that the fourth one was cut by somebody who had stopped learning.
a2_slag_b: A slag sample taken and read over a candle by a hedge-thaumaturge who has been doing this since the Barrow Moor. The mint has been cutting irons continuously for nine hundred years. It stopped, entirely, eleven days ago, and the last of the slag on the heap is still warm enough to prove it.
e_a2_slag_1: A dig into the warmest part of a nine-hundred-year slag heap, which is warm because it is still working. What it has been working on is the mint's other rejects, the ones that were not blanks, and the heap gives way under the digging in the way that a stack of anything gives way under digging.
a2_tallyyard: The tally-yard is working: eleven clerks at standing desks, a weighing floor, and a queue of ward families waiting to have their household counts entered for the month. It is a municipal office. It has a bench for waiting, a rail for queueing, and a jug of water, and everybody in it is entirely calm.
a2_tallyyard_a: The company is entered in the ward's count as five, which a clerk does without looking up from his desk. Then he corrects it, at the bottom of the entry, to nine, without being asked and without explaining. When Nyre asks him why, he says that arrivals are entered at nine, and goes on to the next family.
a2_tallyyard_b: A Warden charter is presented to the head clerk, who reads it, thanks the captain for producing it, files a copy in the correct box, and continues the morning's counting, and a charter is a document. The count is the count. He does not appear to see any conflict between those two facts at all.
e_a2_tallyyard_1: A clerk's desk is tipped over in a working tally-yard in front of eleven clerks and forty families. The queue reforms around it. Two of the waiting families help the clerk pick his papers up, and the ward's own constables arrive within the quarter hour with a form already partly filled in.
a2_scales: The yard's weighing floor holds a dwarf balance with nine pans, in daily use, and it weighs nothing that can be seen. A clerk stands beside it entering a result in a book after each empty weighing, and the ninth pan hangs a quarter of an inch lower than the other eight.
a2_scales_a: The clerk's book, read over his shoulder: nine columns, one per pan, and in each column a name and a weight, and today's ninth column is blank. The pan under it is sitting low, and the clerk is waiting, pen in hand, for whatever it is that fills in the ninth column at the hour.
e_a2_scales_1: A company captain stands on the ninth pan of a dwarf balance in a working tally-yard, which the clerk records without any comment at all. It produces a weight. It also produces a name, entered in the ninth column in the clerk's neat hand, and the name is not the captain's.
a2_clerks: The clerks' hall behind the yard holds eleven people keeping the ward's arithmetic, and at the end desk an old woman who has been copying the crown ledger for forty years. She has kept every copy. She has them in date order in a cupboard behind her, and she is the only person in Kar Ashen who has ever expected to be asked for them.
a2_clerks_a: The copies are handed over without argument by a woman who has waited forty years for somebody to ask for them. She wants a receipt. She writes the receipt herself, in triplicate, and signs all three, and keeps one, and hands the other two to the company with the cupboard's key on top of them.
a2_clerks_b: The answer is given flatly across a desk, without any softening: a household that falls behind is carried by the ward for three months. After three months it is entered in the ninth column. After it is entered in the ninth column it is not a household, and the ward re-allots its rooms.
e_a2_clerks_1: Forty years of crown-ledger copies taken off an old clerk's desk while she is at the yard, which is quicker than asking. It is noticed inside the hour, because she checks the cupboard hourly and has done for forty years. The ward's constables hold the company in the clerks' hall until the crown clerk can come up.
a2_cells: The ward cells under the clerks' hall are nine in a row, and eight of them are occupied by people who have fallen behind and are waiting quietly, with their households' tokens around their necks; the ninth is standing open. It has been swept, and it is warmer than the corridor.
a2_cells_a: Eight cell doors opened with Kettle's picks in under two minutes, and eight people who do not come out, and the arrangement is that they are carried down on the ninth and their households are cleared; they have families in this ward. Two of them ask the company to close the doors again before the count.
a2_cells_b: Eleven minutes through the grilles with eight people who are entirely reconciled to the arrangement and are worried about something else. What worries them is whether the company's arrival will disrupt the schedule. A disrupted schedule means arrears, and arrears fall on the households that are still standing.
a2_cells_c: The ninth cell, looked into: swept, warm, empty, with nine tally-marks cut into the plaster at eye height and a fresh tenth begun. The sweeping has been done from the inside, which is clear from the direction of the marks in the dust, and the tenth mark is at the height of a man's shoulder.
e_a2_cells_1: The ninth cell is entered deliberately and its door pulled to, because somebody in this company needed to know what a swept cell is for. The ninth hour arrives exactly on schedule to collect what is in it. The tenth tally-mark is finished from the outside, afterwards, by whoever does the finishing.
e_a2_cells_2: Eight people are carried out of ward cells over their own objections and their families' objections both. The ward does not fight the company for them. The schedule appoints eight others by the ninth hour, and it adds the carriers to the list, because the list has always had a provision for carriers.
a2_cistern: The cistern channel under the outer ward is a dwarf conduit four feet high running full, with an inspection grating every hundred feet. The water in it is warm and comes down from somewhere above the city. It does not smell of stone. Everybody notices that at the same moment and nobody says it out loud.
a2_cistern_a: A quarter mile waded upstream in warm water against a current that has come off something the size of a mountain. It arrives under the ward at a grating that lifts from below, which means somebody uses it from this side and has greased the hinge. Everybody's legs are warm afterwards for an hour.
a2_cistern_b: The maintenance ledge above the water is eleven inches wide and slick with nine centuries of mineral, and it is taken in the dark with the current going the other way underneath. Halt slips at the third grating and is caught by Hask. The catching is the loudest thing that happens in the conduit.
e_a2_cistern_1: The warm water is followed downstream instead of up, on the entirely reasonable grounds that the source is what matters and the source can be found from either end. The conduit's outfall is where the ward's ninth-hour deliveries go, and the company arrives at it four minutes before the hour does.
a2_drowned: The drowned quarter under the ward is eleven streets of dwarf housing flooded to the lintels, with lamps burning above the waterline in every ninth window. There is a boat chained at the steps and a pole beside it. The water is warm, and the lamps are trimmed, and nobody is at any of the windows.
a2_drowned_a: A chained boat cut loose and poled down eleven flooded streets, past lit ninth windows with nobody at them; the water is warm and does not smell the way water smells. Nyre reads the street names off the door lintels as they pass and stops reading them aloud at the fourth street.
a2_drowned_b: The shallow street by the temple wall is thigh-deep the whole way, and the temple's east wall carries a tally in groups of nine from the waterline right up to the roof line. The lower groups are underwater and legible through it, which means the water arrived after the counting started and did not stop it.
a2_drowned_c: The roofs of the drowned quarter are crossed above the water in the dark, dwarf slate holding under boots the whole way. From up there the ward's whole lamplight is visible, and nine of the windows below are lit, and their pattern across eleven streets is not random and is not a pattern of habitation.
e_a2_drowned_1: A lit ninth-window house is broken into above the waterline. Inside there is a table laid for nine, with a ninth place set and untouched. The other eight places are occupied by the household that fell behind three months ago and has been carried since, and all eight of them look up at once.
e_a2_drowned_2: The boat is put in at one of the lit houses on the way past, because a lamp in a window means somebody, and somebody might be helped. The somebody turns out to be the arrangement rather than a household. It is a considerable relief for the first four seconds, and then it is not.
a2_pumps: The ward pump house still works: nine dwarf pumps in a row with three of them turning, and a maintenance book that has been kept faithfully by hand for nine hundred years; the book is on a shelf, in date order, in nine volumes. The current volume is open at today's page and today's page is filled in.
a2_pumps_a: The maintenance book, read from the back: nine hundred years of entries, one hand per century, every bearing and every repack recorded. The current hand starts eleven days ago, in the middle of a page, without any handover note. In nine hundred years of this book that has never happened before.
a2_pumps_b: A dwarf toolkit taken out of a working pump house: spanners, a bearing puller, and a spool of the wire the dwarves used for gauge work. Vurma values the wire above everything else the company has picked up in three books and says so, and lashes it inside her own coat rather than to the barrow.
e_a2_pumps_1: Three working pumps are stopped in a pump house that has kept eleven streets from filling for nine hundred years. The water is coming up through the drowned quarter's roofs inside the hour. The ward's response is to send its constables to the pump house rather than to the water, which tells the company who it is dealing with.
a2_eels: The eel channel behind the pump house is a dwarf sluice full of pale eels nine feet long, farmed by the ward and fed on a rota, and a farmer stands on the walkway with a bucket at the ninth hour; the walkway is eleven inches wide. The bucket is heavy enough that he carries it with both hands.
a2_eels_a: The walkway is crossed with a farmer's bucket going into the channel alongside, and eleven feet of pale eel coming up out of the water for the contents. The contents are not fish, and were not fish yesterday either. Nobody in the company looks down after the first look, and Mira does not look at all.
a2_eels_b: The farmer answers the way a man answers a trade question: the eels take what the ward's ninth column allots, and he has farmed them for thirty years and his father did before him, and the yield feeds four streets. He is proud of the yield, and there is no reason for him not to be.
a2_eels_c: An hour on the walkway watching the ninth-hour feed from beginning to end, which is what it takes to understand the arithmetic properly. By the end of it the company knows what the ward's count is, what it is for, and what happens to the part of it that the eels do not take.
e_a2_eels_1: Nine feet of pale eel is attacked in its own sluice by a company that has had enough of the arrangement, on a walkway eleven inches wide, with eight more eels in the water. The first one is killed. It is in the water rather than out of it by then, and so is the person who killed it.
e_a2_eels_2: The farmer is asked whose turn the bucket was, and he answers, and the name is one the company heard through a cell grille an hour ago. He waits politely for the next question with the empty bucket in his hands, and the next question does not come, because nobody in the company can find it.
a2_barracks: The ward's garrison barracks on the wall holds forty bunks with twenty occupied, and the militia in it salutes a Warden charter properly. The sergeant has held this wall for the crown clerk for nineteen years. He is competent, his men are turned out, and his standing orders are on the wall in a frame.
a2_barracks_a: The ward goes under Warden orders on paper, which the sergeant accepts, salutes and files. Then he explains, without any insolence at all, that the order cannot be executed, because the militia's count is kept by the crown clerk and not by him. A man cannot be ordered out of a column he is entered in.
a2_barracks_b: The answer is given on the wall itself, with the sergeant pointing outward and then downward. Not the road, and not the spine. What his militia holds this wall against is the ninth-hour file coming up out of the city below, and his whole standing order, framed on his wall, is to let it through.
e_a2_barracks_1: A ward militia sergeant is arrested on a Warden charter in his own barracks in front of twenty of his men. The twenty do not intervene, which is worse than if they had. The crown clerk's constables arrive within the hour to take custody of everybody in the room, including the charter.
a2_wall: The ward wall's inner walk looks down over the city proper, and the city proper is lamplit all the way to a darkness at its centre that the lamps stop short of. Four things in Warden cloaks are coming up the stair to the walk, in step, at a marching pace, and the walk is eleven feet wide.
a2_wall_a: A stair head held with shields against four things that fight like drilled men, because that is what they were; it costs blood and it buys the walk. Afterwards Dellach sits down on the parapet and says that the third one used a Warden's fourth-form guard on him, correctly, and that he learned it in the same school.
a2_wall_b: The barracks door is taken at a run, and twenty militia close it behind the company and then stand at their posts as though nothing at all is passing on the walk outside. Something passes on the walk outside. It takes about ninety seconds, and not one of the twenty looks at the door.
a2_wall_c: The road is given and the company stands aside against the parapet while four of them go past in step, close enough to touch, close enough to smell the lamp oil in their cloaks; none of the four turns a head. The fourth one is a foot shorter than the others and wearing a militia issue belt.
e_a2_wall_1: The parapet is gone over onto the drowned quarter's roofs in the dark, which is nine-hundred-year-old dwarf slate over eleven feet of warm water. It has been holding that water in the dark for a long time without being walked on, and it does not object at the first boot or the second.
e_a2_wall_2: Four of them are followed back down the stair into the city proper, which is where they were going anyway. At the bottom of the stair the rest of the shift is forming up for the ninth hour, in a yard, in nines, and the company arrives in the middle of the forming up.
a2_bell: The ward bell tower holds a dwarf bell the height of a man, rung on the ninth hour every ninth day; its rope has been spliced by nine generations of ringers and every splice is different. The ringer's log hangs on a nail beside the rope, and it is full, and it has entries in it for next month.
a2_bell_a: The bell rope is cut and coiled, nine generations of splices in forty feet of hemp, which is a museum in a bag; it stops nothing at all. The ward's ringers keep a spare rope and have kept one since the founding, and it is on the shelf under the log, and the ringer offers to fetch it.
a2_bell_b: The bell is rung once, off the hour, which empties the ward's streets in ninety seconds. Four hundred people go indoors without hurrying and without shouting, in the manner of a town that has drilled this. Then the crown clerk's constables arrive at the tower door with a form and no particular urgency.
e_a2_bell_1: The bell is left alone and the tower's own log is read instead, which lists every ringing for nine hundred years. Tomorrow's ninth-hour ringing is already entered, with the ringer's name against it. So is the company's number, in the column the log keeps for what the ringing is for.
a2_billet: The ward's travellers' house is clean and warm, with nine beds in the room, and eight are stripped; the ninth is made up, unoccupied, and kept that way, with the blanket turned down. The housekeeper says the room sleeps eight and does not explain the ninth bed, and does not appear to think it needs explaining.
a2_billet_a: A night in a warm ward billet with four beds used and the ninth left made. Nothing happens. Everybody sleeps better than they will admit to in the morning, and in the morning the ninth bed has been slept in and remade, and the housekeeper has already changed the linen and does not mention it.
a2_market: The ward market at midday sells bread, iron, rope, and lamp oil by the ninth. There is a stall selling tally-blanks to households the way a stall elsewhere sells nails: in bundles, by gauge, with a discount for quantity. The stallholder has a queue and a ledger and a boy to run errands.
a2_market_a: The blank-seller answers as a tradesman answers: households buy them for the ninth-column entries, one per name. He has sold four hundred this season, he expects to sell nine more today, and he keeps a book because the crown clerk's household audits him. He is entirely willing to show anybody the book.
a2_market_b: Nine blanks bought at market price with a written receipt in the seller's own hand, itemised, dated and signed. It costs eleven pence. It is, on any reasonable assessment, the single plainest piece of evidence anybody has taken off this mountain in three books, and it fits in a coat pocket.
e_a2_market_1: The blank stall is turned over in a working market, and four hundred people stop what they are doing, and then they pick the blanks up, one at a time, and hand them back to the seller. It takes about four minutes. Afterwards they all look at the company, and go on looking, and nobody says anything.
a2_beggars: The ward's uncounted sit at the market's edge and are in no column at all: nine of them, fed on the market's leavings, entirely willing to talk to strangers for bread. They are not treated badly. They are simply not in the arithmetic, and the arithmetic is what the ward means by being a person.
a2_beggars_a: Bread bought and an hour given, and nine uncounted deliver the ward's history from underneath: which families were cleared, in which years, what the crown clerk's hand looks like, and which of the ward's officials can be relied on. It is better intelligence than the Wardens have collected in nineteen years.
e_a2_beggars_1: The question about becoming uncounted is asked, and the oldest of the nine answers it in one sentence: you are uncounted when your name has been entered and taken. Then he says, without any drama at all, that this is true of all nine of them, and that two of them were taken this spring.
a2_gaol: The ward gaol is not the cells: it is a proper stone gaol with a gaoler, a book, and four prisoners in for ordinary crimes. At the end of the row there is a Warden in a cell who has been there since autumn, and whose entry in the gaol book has no charge written against it.
a2_gaol_a: A Warden of Thane's own command comes out of a ward gaol on a charter, four months in, thin and entirely lucid. He can name every officer of the crown clerk's household from memory, in order of seniority, with the hours they keep. He has had four months in a stone room to memorise it.
a2_gaol_b: Eleven minutes through a cell door with a man who has had four months to arrange what he would say if anybody ever came, and the hours, and the file, and the crown clerk; where the mint's die is kept and who holds the key to the rack. He says all of it twice, in the same order, to be sure it is remembered.
e_a2_gaol_1: A Warden is left in a ward gaol because a prisoner is a burden on a mountain, which is defensible and which the gaoler writes in his book as the company declining custody. The crown clerk reads that entry the same evening. He now knows the company came, looked at his prisoner, and left him there.
a2_keeper: The ward's lamp-keeper holds the oil rota and the hour book, and is the only person in Kar Ashen who can say precisely when the ninth hour falls, because the hour is not the sun's hour and never has been; she is nine years old. Her mother held the book before her and taught her the reckoning.
a2_keeper_a: The hour book is handed over by a nine-year-old on the strength of a Warden charter she cannot read, because a charter is a grown-up thing and she has been taught to cooperate with grown-up things. It has the rota for the next nine days in it, and a note in an adult hand about the crown door.
a2_keeper_b: The answer comes from a child who does not understand that any of it is remarkable, and her mother taught her the reckoning, and her mother was taught by the crown clerk himself, who teaches every keeper personally. She has met him twice. She says he is kind and that he checks her arithmetic.
e_a2_keeper_1: An hour book is taken off a nine-year-old lamp-keeper without asking. She reports it, because reporting it is her job and she was taught the reporting along with the reckoning. The crown clerk's household is on the ward stair within the hour, and it arrives at the walking pace it always uses.
a2_yardmaster: The yardmaster of the outer ward administers four hundred people and their counts, and he has been expecting a Warden company since the ninth station's book was signed. He has tea ready and two chairs set out. He is neither stupid nor cruel, and he has run this ward for nineteen years without a riot.
a2_yardmaster_a: Two hours of tea and justification from a man who has thought about it more than anybody in the company has, and the ward is fed, warm, lit and safe. Nobody is taken who has not fallen behind. And the alternative, he says, setting down his cup, is Hollowmarch, and he can describe Hollowmarch, and he does.
a2_yardmaster_b: The charter goes on the table and the ward is formally under Warden authority, which the yardmaster accepts with visible relief and enters in his own book with the time. Then he explains what it changes about the ninth hour, which is nothing, and asks whether the company would like to see the rota.
e_a2_yardmaster_1: The question is asked of a yardmaster about his own position if the count fails, and he answers it honestly, because he has answered every other question honestly. He is the ninth column's first entry and has been for nineteen years. That is what the office is. That is why nobody else applied for it.
a2_stores: The ward stores hold nine hundred years of grain, oil and salt in dwarf bins, better stocked than Sarnhold and better kept. There is a written allocation for every household on the wall. There are also nine bins at the end of the row that are not allocated to anybody, and the storekeeper's list skips them.
a2_stores_a: The nine unallocated bins are opened, and eight are full of founding-gauge blanks packed in chaff, and the ninth is full of household goods: boots, coats, a child's mitten, sorted by size and stacked in nines. It is not a store of the dead's belongings. It is a store of the not-yet, sorted in advance.
a2_stores_b: A month of stores drawn and signed for at ward prices, which the storekeeper enters without comment and totals correctly. It is the last honest transaction anybody in the company makes in Kar Ashen. The storekeeper insists on giving the correct change for it, in ward coin, counted twice.
e_a2_stores_1: The oil bins are fired to burn a rota, in a stone city with nine hundred years of oil in it. The fire does not spread, because dwarf stores are cut to contain exactly this and every bin has its own stone lip. What it does is tell four hundred people what the company is, in one afternoon, permanently.
a2_kiln: The ward kiln is hot and tended, with a firing on: nine saggars in the chamber and a kiln-master who will not open it before the hour. He cannot say what is in the saggars, and he means that literally. He loads what he is given, fires it, and hands over what comes out, and has for eleven years.
a2_kiln_a: A kiln opened four hours early, which ruins the firing and the kiln-master's month. Inside are nine saggars, and in each saggar a set of tally-blanks bedded in sand, and every blank already cut with a name. The names are in a hand the company has now seen in four fortresses and one mint.
a2_kiln_b: Two hours of waiting with a kiln-master who talks about clay the entire time, cheerfully and at length. The firing is drawn at the proper hour and nine saggars are opened in front of the company by a man who genuinely did not know what he has been firing, and who has to sit down afterwards.
a2_kiln_c: The kiln-master's book, given willingly: nine firings a season, one on each ninth day, and the same nine names entered as the customer every single time for nineteen years. He has never met the customer. The order comes down with the clay, and the clay comes from the crown clerk's household.
e_a2_kiln_1: Nine saggars are broken in a hot kiln chamber with a moor-iron pick, which destroys nine sets of cut blanks and takes about a minute. The ward's arithmetic treats destroyed blanks as arrears rather than as a loss. Arrears fall on whoever is nearest to them, and the company is standing in the kiln chamber.
e_a2_kiln_2: A saggar's contents are taken out of a working kiln: nine cut blanks in sand, still hot enough to need gloves. The ninth blank in the set is cut with a name that the captain has been carrying in a pack since Gallowmere, and it is cut properly, in the founding hand, with the correct rank.
a2_watch: The ward watch house stands at the head of the deep stair and keeps the city's own log; the log for tomorrow has already been written, in the crown clerk's hand, and it is on the desk under a rule. The watch sergeant does not stop the company reading it and does not offer it either.
a2_watch_a: Tomorrow's entry, read at a watch house desk: the ninth-hour file, its numbers, its route through the ward, and at the bottom of the page a company of five entered as arriving at the crown door. The hour against that last entry has been left blank, and the blank has been ruled, ready.
e_a2_watch_1: The city log is taken off a watch house desk and carried down the deep stair, because the log is the case. The watch reports it at once, because the log is the city and a city cannot be without its log. The company goes down into Kar Ashen with the whole city awake behind it.
a2_deepstair: The deep stair at the ward's inner edge is nine feet wide and cut for traffic, dropping in long flights into the counted city itself; there is lamplight all the way down, on both walls, at intervals. The air coming up is warm and smells of forge and stone and something underneath both of those.
